description:
We’re a group of motivated students from KTECH and KETCH excited to take on challenges, share ideas, and build something amazing together at NASA Space Apps Challenge!

We’re looking for creative, passionate, and team-oriented students with skills in coding, design, research, science, or problem-solving. Most importantly, we value teamwork, curiosity, and a willingness to learn.

Open exclusively to KTECH and KETCH students. Let’s learn, create, and make an impact together!
summary:
ASTER is a junior astronaut mission trainer for children aged 7 to 12. The player wakes up at ASTER Base on Mars and lives one real Mars day, May 20, 2024, the day a real solar storm reached the planet. Three useful jobs compete for one battery: growing food, keeping the crew safe from the storm, and sending research home. The child makes each choice by hand at a console, sees what it costs, and can replay the same day to try for a better result.

Every number that matters comes from NASA: the storm is NASA's own archived record of that event, the power budget follows from Mars receiving 43% of Earth's sunlight, and the message delay is the real distance between Earth and Mars. Around the mission, an Academy of short films and hands-on lessons teaches the ideas, and a flyable Solar System shows where it all sits. It matters because children are told that space is hard; ASTER lets them feel why, safely, with real data, and still win.
details:
**What it does**

ASTER has three connected parts, and one certificate that all three fill.

- **Outpost Mission (the trainer).** A day at ASTER Base in three steps. Morning: set the greenhouse lights. Midday: a solar storm is coming, get the crew into the storm shelter before it arrives. Evening: spend the last spare power on the next crop or on sending the day's research to Earth, aiming the dish yourself. A day is won when the crew is safe and the air runs all night; up to three stars reward meeting the food and research goals too. The result screen shows what each choice changed and names the one step to change next time.

- **Academy (the classroom).** Six one-minute narrated films (the Sun, the planets, orbits and moons, black holes, comets and asteroids, the Milky Way), five hands-on lessons (why Mars is dimmer, how long a message takes, gravity on other worlds, recycling water, power through the night), and a 38-word glossary. Each fact shows its NASA source.

- **Solar System (the playground).** Fly a ship between eight worlds under NASA's real star map, scan them and collect discoveries. Sizes and distances are squeezed by a stated rule; directions are where the planets really are today.

**How the parts connect**

The Academy teaches an idea, the mission makes the child use it under pressure, and the Solar System shows where it sits. A lesson explains that sunlight at Mars is 43% of Earth's; in the mission that number is why the battery cannot pay for everything. A lesson times a message from Earth to Mars; in the mission that wait is the cost of sending research home. Patches earned in all three parts fill one Junior Astronaut certificate, issued to a call sign so no child's name is typed or stored.

**Who it is for**

Children aged 7 to 12, at home with a controller or keyboard, and the teachers, parents, museum educators and club leaders who run sessions for them. A full mission day takes about ten minutes, so it fits a lesson.

**How it works**

- Built in Unreal Engine 5.8 in C++.

- The mission is a small simulation with no engine dependencies, so its rules are tested on their own: 60 unit tests, plus 15 automated tests inside the engine.

- All teaching content is data: 57 facts, each stored with its NASA or partner-agency page and a word-for-word excerpt that a script re-checks against the live page; 86 caption lines; the films and lessons are built from those.

- Accessibility: every spoken line is also a caption, text size can be raised, the game plays fully from a controller, and nothing depends on colour alone or on sound alone.

**Benefits and what we hope to achieve**

Children practise the thing astronauts actually do most: deciding what to spend a scarce resource on, with consequences. They meet real NASA measurements as inputs to a decision, not as trivia. We hope ASTER can be used in classrooms and science clubs in Kuwait and beyond as a ten-minute, replayable introduction to mission thinking, and that the same structure can carry new mission days built from other real events in NASA's records.

**Tools, languages, hardware and software**

Unreal Engine 5.8, C++17, Python (data, checks, editor automation), Blender (scripted modelling of the game's own consoles), GoogleTest, CMake, Git. Text-to-speech: Kokoro-82M through kokoro-onnx. Hardware: a Windows laptop with an NVIDIA RTX GPU; a PlayStation 5 controller.

## Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

Yes.

- **Code and data.** AI coding assistants (Claude Code) wrote most of the C++ game code, the Python and Blender scripts that build and check the game's content, and the editor automation. The repository's readme and commit history say so; commits made with the assistant are marked "Co-Authored-By".

- **Text.** AI drafted the captions, briefings, lesson text and glossary wording. Every stated fact was then tied to a NASA page and a word-for-word excerpt that a script verifies.

- **Audio.** The narration is AI-generated speech: Kokoro-82M text-to-speech, run locally, one adult voice. No person was recorded and no child's voice is used. This is stated in the in-game credits, in the transcript, and in each audio file's metadata.

- **Images, video and 3D models.** The logo and ui ux design and some 3d assets and configuration .

## NASA Data

ASTER uses NASA data as inputs to its mission, not only as citations.

**From this challenge's resource list**

- **Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information (DONKI).** The mission day is built on DONKI's archived record of the May 2024 solar storm at Mars: WSA-ENLIL simulation 30938, the coronal mass ejection of 2024-05-16 13:38 UTC, with predicted arrival at Mars on 2024-05-20 06:40 UTC. That arrival is the storm the player must shelter from. The record is stored in the game with its retrieval date and is labelled "historical", never shown as live. https://ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/DONKI/view/WSA-ENLIL/30938/-1

**Other NASA data and resources**

- **NSSDCA Mars, Moon, Sun and Planetary Fact Sheets.** Solar irradiance at Mars (586.2 against Earth's 1361.0 W/m², a ratio of 0.431) sets the base's solar power in every step of the mission; Mars gravity and the length of a sol are used in the lessons. https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/

- **JPL Solar System Dynamics, Approximate Positions of the Planets.** The game computes where each planet is today and the Earth–Mars distance on the mission day. That distance is the radio delay the player pays for when sending research. https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/planets/approx_pos.html

- **"NASA Watches Mars Light Up During Epic Solar Storm".** The Curiosity rover's radiation reading from the same storm ("equivalent to 30 chest X-rays") is what the player is shown if the crew is caught outside. https://www.nasa.gov/solar-system/planets/mars/nasa-watches-mars-light-up-during-epic-solar-storm/

- **Mars 2020 Perseverance, Sounds of Mars.** The wind heard at the base is the rover's real recording, captioned as such. https://science.nasa.gov/mission/mars-2020-perseverance/sounds-of-mars/

- **NASA imagery.** Earth (Blue Marble, Black Marble, cloud map), the Moon (LROC), Mars (Viking mosaic), Jupiter's large moons (Voyager and Galileo mosaics, JPL/USGS), and the sky (NASA SVS Deep Star Maps 2020).

- **NASA Science, NASA.gov and NASA Space Place pages** behind the facts in the films, lessons and glossary, including "Growing Plants in Space", "The Human Body in Space", "NASA Achieves Water Recovery Milestone on International Space Station", "Sun: Facts", "Planets", "Black Holes", "Comets", "Asteroids" and "Meteors and Meteorites".

The full register, with every excerpt, is `Documentation/NASA_DATA.md` in the source.

**What is not NASA data, and is labelled so in the game:** the power, food and research units and how choices move them are training assumptions; Mercury, Venus, the giant planets and Titan have representative appearances; the Solar System's sizes and distances are compressed.

## Space Agency Partner Data and Other References

**Engine and tools**

Unreal Engine 5.8 (Epic Games); Blender; Python; GoogleTest; CMake; Kokoro-82M text-to-speech (Apache 2.0) with kokoro-onnx; ffmpeg.

**Art and sound used in the game**

- KitBash3D, Mission to Minerva (props, solar arrays, rover).

- Jonathon Frederick, Modular SciFi Season 1 and Season 2 Starter Bundles (the base's rooms and props).

- Lumax Studio, Sci-Fi Lite Sample Pack (antenna, work stations).

- ErikGames, Medical Clinic and Laboratory Futuristic Sci-Fi (comms room equipment).

- avrenworks, Sci-Fi Bed (crew bunks).

- ProMaxx Studio, Sci-Fi Trooper Man v.3 (the cadet). RAISOR 4096, Sci-Fi Soldier 02 (the crew).

- Arghanion, Space Ship Flight System; Corinth Cargo Transporter by Yvo Pors, CC BY 4.0, modified by Arghanion.

- Mars terrain, sky, planet materials and some base props: third-party assets used with their author's permission. [Team: the guide asks that all external resources be listed here. Name these two asset sets here unless their author still prefers otherwise, and make sure the permission tick box is true for every pack above.]

- Music: Traumatic Pixel, Aurora Sound Track.

- Footstep sounds: Kenney (CC0).

- Fonts: Space Grotesk by Florian Karsten and Inter by Rasmus Andersson, SIL Open Font License.

**Made for ASTER**

The mission consoles, room signs, screen artwork, interface and interface sounds; all game code and scripts; all captions and lesson text.

**Space Agency Partner resources**

- **Canadian Space Agency, "Growing healthy food in space and in remote areas"** (from the CSA food-production toolkit in this challenge's resources): the fact shown at the greenhouse's seed bench, that station crews get fresh food only every few months, so a Mars crew must grow its own. https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/sciences/food-production/growing-healthy-food-in-space-and-remote-areas.asp
